title: Answer of the Virginia State Corporation Commission in opposition to Constellation Energy Generation, LLC's Motion to File Supplemental Comments under EL25-49, et al.

documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.                  )              Docket No. EL25-49-000
                                                     )
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating                 )              Docket No. AD24-11-000
                                                     )
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC                 )
                                                     )
               v.                                    )              Docket No. EL25-20-000
                                                     )              (consolidated)
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                          )

                    ANSWER TO MOTION OF THE VIRGINIA STATE
                          CORPORATION COMMISSION

       Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or the

“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.213, the Virginia State

Corporation Commission (“VSCC”) submits this Answer in opposition to the Motion to File

Supplemental Comments of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) filed in the

above-captioned consolidated proceedings on November 21, 2025 (“Motion” and “Supplemental

Comments”).

       This proceeding pits two groups with entrenched corporate interests against one another.

On one side is Constellation, which insists that the PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) tariff is

unjust and unreasonable because it does not explicitly permit the type of co-located generation and

data center arrangement Constellation prefers and financially benefits from. On the other side are

transmission owners, who seek (according to Constellation) to prohibit such arrangements in

service of their own corporate interest of selling transmission service to generators and

interconnected load.
        Caught in the middle are existing customers. If, as Constellation requests, the Commission

permits existing generation assets to exit the market to serve large loads behind-the-meter, the

large load customers get the benefit of partially depreciated, lower cost existing resources while

the remaining customers on the system are forced to pay for higher cost new generation. That is,

new generation built to meet resource adequacy challenges caused almost exclusively by the large

load customers that benefit from Constellation’s proposed arrangement. This scenario, where data

center customers get lower-cost existing generation while everyone else pays for higher cost new

facilities, is the exact opposite of requiring the data centers paying their “fair share” for the costs

they impose. If the Commission permits such a paradigm, it is unequivocally choosing the

corporate interests of a select few over the affordability of electric rates for everyday consumers.

       This complaint, although phrased as a dispute over interconnection, is at its heart a dispute

over retail service arrangements, as data center customers are unquestionably end-use customers

taking retail electric service. Before taking any action regarding co-located load generally or

Constellation’s complaint specifically, the Commission should ensure that the solution to the

problem alleged by Constellation does not make matters worse for retail customers, who are

already facing unprecedented affordability issues posed by large load additions.

       Given that issues related to large load interconnection are under consideration by the

Commission in Docket No. RM26-7-000, that is the appropriate proceeding for the Commission

to carefully consider and craft a solution that enables expeditious large load interconnections

without unfairly burdening consumers with a disproportionate share of the infrastructure costs. In

that proceeding, the VSCC proposed a framework that would address issues related to large load

interconnections, including co-located load, that would obviate the need to take specific PJM

action in this proceeding.



                                                  2
        I.      BACKGROUND

       On November 22, 2024, Constellation filed a complaint under Federal Power Act (“FPA”)

section 206 against PJM in Docket No. EL25-20-000. Constellation asserted in the complaint that

the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) is unjust, unreasonable and unduly

discriminatory because it does not contain rules for governing interconnection of co-located loads.

Constellation requested that the Commission find that the PJM Tariff is unjust, unreasonable and

unduly discriminatory or preferential, and direct PJM to adopt in its Tariff certain portions of

PJM’s Guidance on Co-Located Load.

       On November 1, 2024, the Commission held a technical conference in Docket No AD24-

11-000, to discuss issues related to co-located load. The Commission noted several proceedings in

the PJM Region that involved similar issues. On February 20, 2025, the Commission issued an

order in Docket No. EL25-49-000 (the “Show Cause Order”), instituting a proceeding under FPA

section 206. The Show Cause Order directed PJM and its Transmission Owners to either “(1)

show cause as to why the Tariff, the Amended and Restated Operating Agreement of PJM, and

Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities in the PJM Region remain just

and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential due to the lack of provisions

specifically addressing colocation arrangements;” or (2) explain what changes to these governing

documents would remedy the identified concerns if the Commission were to determine that the

governing documents have become unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or

preferential and, therefore, proceeds to establish a replacement Tariff.

       On October 23, 2025, the Secretary of the Department of Energy (“Secretary”) directed the

Commission to consider an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“ANOPR”) regarding the

interconnection of large loads to the interstate transmission system and issue a final action by April



                                                  3
 30, 2026.1 On October 27, 2025, the Commission issued a Notice Inviting Comments on the

proposed ANOPR. The VSCC submitted Initial Comments and Reply Comments on the ANOPR

on November 15, 2025 and December 5, 2025, respectively.

        In its comments in Docket No. RM26-4-000, the VSCC requested that the Commission

develop a set of Commission-mandated minimum standards for large load interconnections, while

allowing transmission owners to continue to manage large load interconnection queues with direct

oversight of their state regulatory commissions. The VSCC noted that these guidelines could

permit the accelerated interconnection of large loads that are willing to bring their own generation

or to be co-located with generation by creating a fast-track generator interconnection queue for

those verified generation resources. In its Reply Comments, the VSCC included a specific

proposed set of guidelines that would address large load interconnection (including co-located

load), while respecting state regulatory authority.

        II.      ANSWER

                 A.      Constellation’s Proposal Will Create New Affordability Challenges for
                         Retail Ratepayers and Necessarily Raises Questions of Federal Versus
                         State Jurisdiction Better Suited for Careful Consideration in the
                         Existing ANOPR Docket.

        While Constellation argues that the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable because it does

not properly accommodate the specific co-located arrangement Constellation prefers and

financially benefits from, the VSCC is unaware of any evidence indicating that the PJM tariff,

specifically, is unjust and unreasonable necessitating a PJM-specific solution. Rather, to the extent




1
 Secretary of Energy, Secretary of Energy’s Direction that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Initiate
Rulemaking Procedures and Proposal Regarding the Interconnection of Large Loads Pursuant to the Secretary’s
Authority Under Section 403 of the Department of Energy Organization Act (Oct. 23, 2025) (“ANOPR”).


                                                       4
 Constellation raises a legally cognizable issue for the Commission to resolve, it is how co-located

load should be accommodated generally.

            In its Supplemental Comments, Constellation asserts that the Commission can avoid

jurisdictional arguments by “assert[ing] jurisdiction over hybrid facilities at a shared point of

interconnection. The Commission’s jurisdiction is over the interconnection facilities, not any retail

sale.”2 The actual reality is far more complicated than Constellation asserts, and obviously

implicates state authority over retail sales. For example, Constellation urges the Commission to

reject the argument that its jurisdiction over large load interconnection is limited to where

transmission service is provided to customers as an unbundled product,3 directly asking the

Commission to exercise jurisdiction over a retail sale (that also includes bundled transmission

service).

            In addition, Constellation claims that by only exercising jurisdiction over interconnections,

the Commission need not concern itself with the retail wheeling prohibition in FPA section

212(h).4 Taking this argument to its logical conclusion reveals the absurdity of Constellation’s

argument.          Obviously, customers seeking interconnection are generally seeking such

interconnection to take transmission service. If the customer is not requiring or taking transmission

service, the co-location arrangement can be islanded from the grid. Yet, that is not what

Constellation proposes. If, instead, the large load customer is permitted to take any service from

the transmission system, the interconnection is by its very nature enabling retail wheeling as the

data center is an end-use customer. Moreover, PJM does not have the ability to monitor whether


2
    Supplemental Comments at 13.
3
    Id. at 18.
4
    Id. at 17-18; 18 U.S.C. § 824k(h).


                                                     5
 large load customers served via co-location arrangements are taking retail electric service from a

non-utility provider, even if such sales are prohibited by state law.

          Constellation acknowledges that PJM faces a significant reliability problem. It suggests

that the Commission deal with this problem by “fix[ing] the market so it is better able to respond

to the resource adequacy issue and … fix the load forecast.”5 Constellation is simultaneously

requesting relief in this proceeding that would exacerbate resource adequacy and reliability issues

before the Commission can try to fix the dysfunctional market. In the interim, Constellation and

its co-locating data center customers benefit, while everyone else loses. Constellation reaps an

additional windfall as a co-locating generator and owner of a generation portfolio that will benefit

from a market that is both short of resources and expensive, as the recent PJM capacity auctions

have demonstrated.

          The relief requested by Constellation, which would have the Commission change the PJM

tariff to accommodate the business arrangement Constellation prefers, will have real impact on

non-data center customers at a time those customers are facing significant affordability issues.

Constellation proposes to take existing generation resources that are currently serving customers

off the market and dedicate these resources to a data center customer. These existing resources

are depreciated, and thus significantly cheaper than the new facilities the remaining customers

would have to pay for to replace the departing resource. At a time when state and federal regulators

alike are endeavoring to ensure that data center customers pay their “fair share” of the costs they

impose on the system, Constellation proposes that the Commission do the exact opposite.

          The ANOPR frames these issues, asking whether and, if so, how hybrid loads (including

co-located loads) should be interconnected in all regions. Taking action specific to the PJM region


5
    Supplemental Comments at 31.


                                                  6
 thus appears to be both premature and potentially harmful, to the extent it conflicts with later

guidance through the NOPR process. The Commission should, therefore, reject Constellation’s

request and focus its efforts on the ANOPR.

       As the VSCC noted in its ANOPR comments, by promulgating a set of guidelines for all

large load interconnections to be applied by transmission owners in their state tariffs, the

Commission could remove barriers to all such interconnections, including co-located load. In

addition to directing expedited queues for certain limited types of interconnection (including

hybrid loads), the Commission should act within its existing jurisdiction to accelerate

interconnection of generation needed to support load.

       The VSCC also requested in Docket No. RM26-4-000 that the Commission schedule a

technical conference to hear from all interested parties, including state commissions. To the extent

Constellation has raised valid issues for Commission consideration that were not previously

addressed in Docket No. AD24-11-000, these issues could be taken up in the NOPR technical

conference.

               B.      Should The Commission Choose to Act on Constellation’s Complaint
                       Outside of the ANOPR Proceeding, the Commission Should Preserve
                       State Jurisdiction over Bundled Service and Protect Affordability by
                       Permitting Only New Resources to Serve Co-Located Load Absent
                       Sufficient Impact Studies For Existing Generation.

       The VSCC is not necessarily opposed to co-located load and generator arrangements, and

in the ANOPR proceeding proposed a process for such arrangements to receive expedited

interconnection review. However, these arrangements must protect existing retail customers, else

the arrangement act as a wealth transfer from retail customers to generating interests like

Constellation. The VSCC does not believe that action now is warranted, but if the Commission

chooses to act now, it must take two steps to protect existing retail customers.



                                                 7
            First, the Commission should make clear that co-located arrangements are not a means for

data center loads to bypass restrictions on retail sales in vertically-integrated states like Virginia.

With certain limited exceptions, retail customers in Virginia are required to take service from their

incumbent utility, 6 and the Commission does not have jurisdictional authority to disturb these

arrangements, even in the service of expanding data center interconnection. Vertically integrated

states have made a policy determination that limited access to third-party generation is the best

means to protect captive retail ratepayers, and the Commission should respect that policy choice.

           Second, if a generator proposes to remove an existing generation asset from service to

dedicate the output of the generation to a co-locating data center load, the Commission should

require that the generator be studied in the same manner as a retiring generator, including (if

applicable) reliability must-run or similar arrangements.          Otherwise, the remaining retail

ratepayers (who are losing a generation asset otherwise available to them), will face retail rate

increases.        That these rate increases are matters of retail ratemaking is immaterial – the

Commission should refrain from making the affordability issues these ratepayers face worse in the

interest of protecting Constellation’s business model.

           III.     CONCLUSION

           WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, the VSCC requests that the Commission reject

Constellation’s Motion to Expedite, deny Constellation’s complaint and terminate the Show Cause

proceeding without further action.
